titleStmt.title: Model Driven Timing Analysis for Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: Model Driven Timing Analysis for Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper stresses the difficulty for a system designer to use an appropriate real-time task model for his system, and to choose the associated scheduling analysis tests/dimensioning techniques. We propose a model-based approach tackling this difficulty. We focus on the schedulability analysis tree used by our method in order to help the designer to dimension, and then to validate his system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time computing is spreading more and more in our daily lives through the automotive systems, the multimedia, the telecommunications, etc. A real-time system operates in a dynamic environment and must constantly be adapted to changes in that environment. The correctness of large real-time systems is determined partly by the functional results of computations, and partly by the time at which results are produced: this is corresponding to non-functional requirements.

Nowadays, real-time and embedded systems become more complex, both in the architectural complexity (number of processors, networks, etc.), or the requirement complexity (task criticality, power consumption, etc.). These requirements have to be met in every possible situation. Therefore, real-time systems require an analysis phase, to prove that constraints are respected. The design phase of real-time systems can take place over several years, and designers have to cope with new hardware, new software, and/or new standards during the design process. Then, the smallest design mistake can have have a big impact on the real-time system development costs and the system quality.

Temporal faults are among vulnerabilities which must be detected at an early stage of the life-cycle. So, realtime systems need a temporal analysis phase to prove that temporal constraints are met. Temporal analysis is mainly based on the scheduling analysis theories. However, scheduling analysis is still expensive in terms of design expertise. Furthermore, most real-time system designers do not have the timing analysis skills to choose the appropriate scheduling analysis tests for their designs.

During last decades, many design languages have been developed in a way to facilitate scheduling analysis and make it easier at an early stage, such as AADL [16], UML-MARTE [12], EAST-ADL [6], etc. Despite all these standard design languages, scheduling analysis modeling is still costly in terms of design expertise, in terms of formal validation before analyzing the scheduling side, and in terms of traceability to detect the source of a scheduling error, and also suffers from limits to express real-time complex constraints. There are also different analysis tools which allow to analyze real-time systems like SymTA/S [7], MAST [9], Cheddar [17], etc. Unfortunately, this kind of tools requires a high scheduling analysis knowledge. Moreover, to make sure that the tool interprets the actual model entered by a designer is a non-trivial task. In some cases when scheduling analysis tools are not able to analyze the system, they do not provide the reasons of this inability to analyze the system. This latter is often related to the invalidation of the system structure or it is due to the tool itself which does not support this kind of system structure.

In this paper, we use model driven engineering to suggest a process based on Modeling-oriented Scheduling analysis of Real-Time systems (MoSaRT). This process helps designers to analyze step by step their system designs during the design phase. Then, it allows to avoid temporal design mistakes at an early stage of the life-cycle. To reduce the gap between standardized design languages and analysis tools, MoSaRT allows a designer to conceive the real-time system and to validate its structure. After that, MoSaRT helps the designer to choose the best analysis test which corresponds to the design of the system. The remainder of this article is organized as follows.

In the next section, we discuss the related works and the positioning of our work. Section 3 highlights MoSaRT and its utilization to facilitate temporal analysis. Then, Section 4 presents an example through a case study. Finally, Section 5 summarizes and concludes this article.

div.head: II. REAL-TIME CONCERNS AND RELATED WORKS
div.p: A correct system behavior is ensured by the lasting interaction of a real-time system and a physical process. This interaction is based on a set of parallel and interdependent functionalities. These functionalities are composed of a software layer executed on a hardware layer.

The hardware architecture of real-time and embedded systems has been steadily improved. This architecture consists of a set of physical resources like processors, networks, etc. Hardware architectures can be classified into three broad categories according to their composition: uniprocessor, multiprocessor and distributed architectures. The software layer is composed of the application layer which is represented by a functional model mapped on a task model. Several expressive models were proposed over the years and many of them allow an efficient temporal analysis.

The seminal work of Liu and Layland [8] has proposed a task model where a task is characterized by a few temporal parameters. This kind of task models allows a simple scheduling analysis but it is very limited compared to realistic tasks. When validating a critical real-time system S, starting from the real task system S, S' represents a worst-case task model of the real system S. Then, the worst-case behaviour of the task model S' is analyzed in an acceptable delay. All along this process, if the task model S' semantics are poor (lack of expressiveness), then the way S is modeled leads to a pessimistic feasibility analysis (see Figure 1). Feasibility tests are a set of scheduling algorithms and algebraic methods. Scheduling theory has been originally studied for the basic Liu and Layland task model, and extended to cover more advanced and precise task models. The purpose of a feasibility test is to prove that a software model using a set of hardware resources will always respect real-time requirements. In order to decrease the modeling gap between S and S', to obtain a thin design granularity, many task models were proposed as more general model. For instance, the generalized multiframe task model [3], the non-cyclic recurring task model [2] and the digraph task model [20] are models created to handle fine grain models compared to classical task models.

The problem is that usually the more expressive the model is, the more complex is the feasibility test. Thus, the time complexity of the analysis is a very important point. As an example, testing the schedulability of periodic independent tasks with an implicit deadline using a deadline-driven scheduler on a single processor is a very easy problem and requires a linear time in the number of tasks. A small change in the hardware, software or operational context has a big impact on the temporal analysis. For example, with the same hypothesis, if we consider a fixed-priority scheduling policy, in the case where the periodic tasks are either non strictly periodic, or strictly periodic and released simultaneously. Then, the feasibility problem is NP-hard in the weak sense (pseudo-polynomial feasibility test). But if the tasks are strictly periodic and not released simultaneously, then the feasibility problem is NP-hard in the strong sense, while one could, for test efficiency reasons, choose to use a pseudopolynomial feasibility test as a sufficient (but non-necessary) test for this problem. To help system designers to have a good system dimensioning and to avoid the over-sizing of the hardware resources, several research works have proposed interesting results which must be taken into consideration at an early design phase, such as the sensitivity analysis [21], [4], the priority assignment [1], and the multi-criteria optimization [10].

Figure 1. different task models which depend of pessimism and expressiveness referring to the real system (the size of circles is related to the semantic expressiveness of the model) Currently, many commercial and academic scheduling analysis tools were proposed to help designers during the analysis phase. For example, SymTA/S [7], MAST [9] and Cheddar [17] are based on some classical feasibility tests. They vary in terms of analysis capabilities and supported features. The utilization of these analysis tools provided a simple Yes/No answer to the question "does the system meet all its deadlines?". This kind of information is not efficient and not helpful enough for real-time designers, in particular, when an analysis tool is not able to analyze the system. Sometimes, this inability to analyze a real-time system is due to the violation of architectural requirements for the system to be handled by the tool. Therefore, the architectural verification and temporal validation of real-time systems can be difficult to achieve for system designers. Recently some research works aim at helping designers during the modeling phase in order to get a coherent system architecture. Roquemaurel et al. [5] are interested just in the architectural validation to ensure the architecture coherence by using formal methods and constraint satisfaction problems. Plantec et al. [15] have proposed some design patterns, once the designer respects all rules proposed by the design pattern the scheduling analysis corresponding to this pattern can be be applied [15]. Peres et al. [14] have also proposed a verification method for real-time system by using model checking. These research studies focus on one kind of validation (architectural requirements or temporal requirements) of the real-time systems. Moreover, for those which are interested in real-time scheduling, they do not reduce the gap between the real system and the task model, nor offer the closest scheduling model when the real system does not correspond to an existing analyzable model.

The model driven engineering offers a relative independence to technological changes, a better control of the complexity and a better re-usability of the design elements. For these reasons, MoSaRT (Modeling-oriented Scheduling analysis of Real-Time systems) is based on model driven engineering in order to offer enough concepts and semantics to cover, with few modifications, most exiting temporal analysis models and also the future ones. The purpose of this work is not to propose another design language or another analysis tool, but to reduce the gap between these two sides.

MoSaRT takes into consideration the difficulty confronted by designers to check if the system is analyzable and to choose the appropriate scheduling analysis (validation or dimensioning) depending on model completion phase. Consequently, MoSaRT aims at responding to this kind of questions:
• What are the possible task allocations?

• What is the worst-case task model? • What are the efficient tests to validate it? • Are these solutions exact or pessimistic? • If the system is unschedulable, what needs to be changed to make it schedulable? This paper provides some answers, while also highlighting some MoSaRT capabilities.

div.head: III. MOSART-AIDED REAL-TIME DESIGN
div.p: The Modeling-oriented Scheduling analysis of Real-Time systems (MoSaRT) language is conceived as a domain specific language for modeling the scheduling analysis aspect of a real-time system. Referring to this aspect, the main differences between MoSaRT and other standard design languages are:
• The way that MoSaRT allows to design a real-time system. • The MoSaRT capability to support most kind of formats of real-time properties.

• The MoSaRT capability to verify if a real-time system can be analyzable. • The MoSaRT analysis ability which permits to orient designers to choose the most adapted analysis tests. In the next subsections, we give an overview about each enumerated point.

div.head: A. MoSaRT foundation concepts
div.p: MoSaRT language is used to design a real-time system. This design is based on two layers: the operational layer and the application layer. The operational layer is composed of the hardware model, the software architecture model and the behavioral model of this software architecture. The application layer corresponds to the functional model. Figure 2 shows the different kinds of models and their complementarity offering a set of viewpoints. The implementation of MoSaRT language is based on Ecore [19] which is a scripting language for meta-models1 . Moreover, Ecore is an implementation of the MOF (Model Object Facility) [13] under the integrated development environment Eclipse2 which is a well-equipped framework. MoSaRT elements are organized in a set of packages. Each package contains a set of elements corresponding to a model type (see Figure 3). Unlike other design languages, MoSaRT language allows to design the functional model independently from the operational layer. This means that the presence of the functional model is not mandatory to analyze the system, but it is preferable in some cases where the objective is to obtain a fine grain design, especially for modeling conditional models ("if-then-else" or "switch case"). We have chosen UML concepts (Unified Modeling Language) for modeling a functional model because they are popular and they are well suited to this type of model. All other MoSaRT models are mandatory for modeling realtime system. For modeling the hardware architecture, the HardwarePlatform package contains the relevant elements such as the processors, the communication channels, network routers, etc. The main elements found in a MoSaRT software architecture model (like the tasks, the processes, the local/remote communication resources, etc.) are contained in the SoftwareOperators package. The behavior of the software architecture is designed by SoftwareBehaviour package elements. These behaviour elements allow to design the interaction and the interdependence among the tasks, for example, the precedence relationships, the triggers, the steps, etc. Steps represent the task core elements. They indicate when the task acquires/releases a resource, when it sends/receives data, etc. Thanks to step elements the operational layer can be linked to the application layer without any impact on functional model elements.

div.head: B. Real-time features via MoSaRT
div.p: The RealTimeProperties package (see Figure 3) allows the design of non-functional characteristics. These properties are categorized in many packages. For instance, the RtpUtility-Types package offers some utility elements like intervals, lists, durations, etc. The RtpProtocolsAndPolicies package offers scheduling policies, resource management protocols, etc. The particularity of MoSaRT RealTimeProperties package is that every real-time feature has been implemented as a concept (a generic Ecore class). This allows MoSaRT to cover several complex task models and permits to have an open meta-model which is easily extensible. As an illustration, Figure 4 represents the different formats that a task priority value can be. Figure 4 also shows that a real-time feature can be mentioned as unknown (for example, RtpPriorityType class) in order to be computed at an early design stage (such as, the priority assignment which is a dimensioning technique).

div.head: C. The structural verification via MoSaRT
div.p: Models based on object-oriented modeling are not sufficiently precise. So, they must be consolidated by a set of rules. Every rule is a constraint which must be respected by the structure of the modeled system. To specify these constraints many formal languages can be used. OCL (Object Constraint Language) [11] is the formal language which we have chosen to use with MoSaRT. There are two reasons for this choice. The first one is the clarity and the simplicity of OCL that does not use complex mathematical notations. The second reason is related to the implementation language which is Ecore, this latter operates very well with OCL and allows to enrich the meta-model description (for our case the meta-model is MoSaRT) easily through its textual syntax (see Figure 5). Safety rules guarantee that no erroneous behaviour will happen. Figure 6 shows a case where a safety rule is violated. In this case, a "release step" is preceded by itself. A release step means that a task releases a semaphore after the end of the access to a critical shared resource. The Listing 1 shows the corresponding OCL rule. The second kind of structural rule is the vivacity. This kind of rules is very important to ensure the correctness and completeness of the system global behavior. Figure 7. A part of the behavioral model: A vivacity rule is violated Figure 7 shows an example where a vivacity rule is not respected. MoSaRT offers a possibility to design a system global behavior. This global behaviour contains a set of taskActivity elements where each taskActivity represents a software operator task. The global behavior requires that each taskActivity must be triggered or preceded by another taskActivity. Thus, the taskActivity2 does not respect this rule and that causes a blockage of the system. The Listing 2 shows the corresponding OCL rule.

The respect of all these structural constraints by a system design means that the structure is coherent.
In the next subsection we discuss the scheduling analysis ability rules.

div.head: D. The scheduling analysis ability via MoSaRT
div.p: Once the design structure of the system is coherent, the designer can use the scheduling analysis ability rules in order to know which temporal analysis tests match the system design. The scheduling analysis ability rules represent a set of task model assumptions. These rules are also injected in MoSaRT language as OCL constraints which are not mandatory. The verification of every constraint depends on the accuracy of other constraints. The scheduling analysis ability rules are managed as a decision tree (see Figure 9). For example, MoSaRT first checks if a hardware platform exists. If true, then it will verify if the hardware architecture is uniprocessor, else it will verify if the hardware architecture is multi-processor else it will deduce the hardware architecture is distributed. Every tree exploration leads to scheduling analysis tests or dimensioning analysis tests. The type of a temporal test also depends of the model completion phase (see Figure 10). The tree of rules can be enriched easily in order to cover future task models and then future analysis tests.

In the next section we will focus on the capabilities of MoSaRT in terms of scheduling analysis ability. These capabilities will be presented through a simple case study. In this section, we focus on MoSaRT temporal analysis capabilities through an example based on a simple real-time system (this case study contains an improved part of an example presented in [22]). This system is composed of five independent preemptible tasks. These tasks are executed on a processor using an earliest deadline first scheduling policy (EDF) and they are simultaneous. Every task is characterized by a set of properties. Table I summarizes the main task characteristics, and we can notice that the execution time of Task3 is unknown. 11 shows the design of the real-time system which is treated in this case study. This design is conceived through MoSaRT language. The part (1) represents the software architecture. It contains a set of tasks and the scheduler that schedules these tasks. Part (2) represents the hardware architecture, which is uniprocessor. Finally the part (3) represents the behavior of the software elements. So, this part contains the triggers of the tasks and their activities. Every task activity represents a task element existing in part (1). The unknown execution value of Task3 is also expressed as unknown to indicate that it must be calculated. Due to the space limitations, we only present some relevant properties of the model on Figure 11. Each set of properties is linked to its owner design element. Once the design is ready, one can launch the structural rules in order to check if the system verify its all safety, vivacity and architectural constraints. The design shown in Figure 11 respects all these rules. Thus, the design is analyzable. So, the next step is to check the schedulabilty of the system. For this purpose, we use the scheduling analysis rules tree which is presented on Figure 9. As a result, the designer is informed that the system design requires a dimensioning techniques because the execution time value of Task3 is unknown. MoSaRT suggests to a designer to use the sensitivity analysis technique which is presented by Zhang et al. [22]. If this technique was implemented by a third-party tool, the MoSaRT model could be transformed automatically into the input model of this tool (for the purpose of this paper, we did this process by hand). Figure 12 presents the result that is found after running the algorithm which implements the corresponding dimensioning technique: the maximum allowed worst-case execution time for Task3 cannot exceed "13.75 ms". This result can then be integrated by the designer in order to complete his model. In the future, this step should also be automatized. Figure 13 shows an excerpt of the properties of taskActiv-ity3 element which is presented previously in Figure 11. This properties change is directly following the dimensioning analysis through the third-party tool. MoSaRT also keeps the fact that this value has been calculated, and which tool was used, in order for the designer to use several analysis tools and then to compare the received calculated values.

After this design phase, a modeling can be considered complete. Once the designer chose an execution time value which is not greater than "13.75 ms", the designer can analyze the system design by launching the scheduling analysis rules for a second time. This action gives the nearest worst-case task model. In this example, the task model proposed by the decision tree is based on the following assumptions:
• dynamic priority scheduling • arbitrary deadlines • periodic tasks Therefore, as results, MoSaRT proposes to a designer the possible scheduling analysis tests which are [18]:

• the feasibility test based on the processor utilization factor • the feasibility test based on worst-case response time MoSaRT suggests also the prospective analysis tools which propose these feasibility tests like Cheddar, Mast, etc. Figure 14 shows the results given by the Cheddar analysis tool. So, referring to Cheddar analysis results, we can conclude that the real-time system which is treaded in this case study is schedulable.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper we presented a modeling-oriented scheduling analysis of real-time systems. The objective of this approach is to assist designers throughout the design process in order to avoid temporal wrong design choices at an early design stage. Then, designers can gain in term of "time-to-market" especially for critical systems. The aim of this work is not to propose a new design language instead of existing standard design languages nor to propose a new scheduling analysis tool. However, our purpose is on the one hand to overcome the lack of expressiveness of design languages and on the other hand to offer to a designer a panel of different analysis tools in order to choose the most appropriate one and to compare the analysis results. For these reasons, we are working on the model transformations. The first type of transformations will be from standard languages to MoSaRT. The second type will be from MoSaRT to other analysis tools to widen the choice.
